question.leadin: In trying to escape from the capital of this empire, Spanish soldiers experienced La Noche Triste [la no-chay tree-stay].
question.text: Name this empire, led by Montezuma, which was conquered by Hernan Cortes in 1521.
question.clue: Humans were sacrificed in the Templo Mayor of this empire's capital city to please the rain god Tlaloc .

swap.leadin: Following this man's death, hundreds of Spaniards died trying to flee during La Noche Triste [noh-chay tris-tay].
swap.text: Name this leader who was allegedly stoned to death by his own people after being taken hostage by conquistadors.
swap.answerHtml: Montezuma II (accept Moctezuma II; prompt on “Montezuma” or “Moctezuma” alone)
swap.clue: Shortly after this man's death, his people assassinated the rearguard of an invading force in the Night of Sorrows massacre.

question.leadin: Answer these questions about the native peoples of the Americas.
question.text: Sites from this Mesoamerican civilization include La Venta and San Lorenzo, which were mysteriously abandoned. They created giant stone heads, thought to be depictions of their rulers.
question.clue: This culture created "elongated man" figurines as well as a greenstone statue of a man holding a were-jaguar ("wair-jaguar").

swap.text: This Mesoamerican culture played the ballgame in remembrance of the mythical Hero Twins, who played it to escape Xibalba ("shee-BAL-bah"). Thirteen ballcourts were built by this culture at its site of Chichen Itza on the Yucatan Peninsula.
swap.clue: A revolt of these people began a fifty-year long Caste War in the second half of the 19th century.

question.leadin: Name the following historical Mesoamerican civilizations.
question.text: This people's preclassic capital was Mirador, and they were ruled by the kuhul ajaw, mystical kings who claimed to be divine. They mysteriously disappeared after their capital Tikal collapsed.
question.clue: King Pacal of these people was born on 9.8.9.13.0 in this people's "Long Count" calendar.

swap.leadin: The Dresden and Madrid codices contain this culture's writing, and their cities include Palenque (puh-LEN-kay) and Yaxchilan (YAA-shee-lan).
swap.text: Name this civilization, whose Long Count calendar allowed it to mark dates longer than the 52-year "round" used by its 260 and 365-day calendars.
swap.clue: The Temple of Inscriptions houses anajaw("ah-how")from this civilizationknown as Pacal the Great who reigned for 68 years in its city-state of Palenque("pah-LEN-kay").

question.text: Inscriptions in this city lead by Pakal the Great indicate it went into a star war with another in 672 CE. An overgrown jungle in Chiapas now partly covers this city where the ball game was probably played near the Temple of the Inscriptions.
question.clue: The French explorer Jean-Frederic Waldeck resided for a time at this city, where a leafy corn plant mural is located at its "foliated cross" complex.

swap.leadin: Answer the following history bonus somewhat related to soccer, your head editor's favorite sport.
swap.text: Courts for this widespread ritualistic game have been found throughout the Americas, whose modern version is called ulama. Players of this game probably used their hips, though some may have also used rackets or bats.
swap.clue: Participants in this activity attached thin stone heads resembling ax blades to heavy belts known as yokes.

question.text: A ball court can be found at Monte Alban, a city in Oaxaca (wah-HAH-kuh) formerly occupied by the Mixtec and this culture, which carved "danzante" images of captured opponents.
question.clue: The chief god of this culture was the thunder god Cocijo.

swap.leadin: Camilla Townsend used only texts in this language to write her "New History," Fifth Sun.
swap.text: Name this language used in the right columns of the Florentine Codex, where it parallels a translation of the same text in a European language.
swap.clue: Historians learned to write in this language at schools called calmecacs ("kahl-MAY-kahks").

question.text: The final section of the Florentine Codex adopts the perspective of Tenochtitlan in describing the conquest of the Aztec Empire by this Spanish conquistador.
question.answerHtml: Hernán Cortés [or Hernán Cortés de Monroy y Pizarro Altamirano]
question.clue: This man won the Battle of Otumba and fathered a child with his translator, La Malinche.

swap.leadin: Civilizations utilizing this system also used a smaller-scale system with Haab' and Tzolk'in components.
swap.text: Identify this primarily base-20 system. The end of a b'ak'tun was predicted by this system's Long Count.
swap.clue: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel discusses this system, which was split into the divine Tzolk'in and civil Haab' derived from "Venus rounds."

question.leadin: This city's emblem glyph is the most widely distributed of all such glyphs in the Americas.
question.text: Name this city whose ruler Sky Witness achieved a major power reversal by converting Caracol from a vassal of this city's rival Tikal into an ally. Today, this city is identified as the capital of the "Kingdom of the Snake."
question.clue: This Snake Kingdom known for being the bitter enemy of Tikal during the Classical Mayan period.

swap.leadin: A series of figures constructed by this civilization were unearthed by Matthew and Marion Stirling.
swap.text: Name this civilization whose art frequently featured the were-jaguar motif. Colossal stone heads constructed by this civilization were found at sites such as San Lorenzo and La Venta.
swap.clue: Much of their art is based on a jaguar god, including much in that capital, La Venta.

question.text: The two classes of elite Aztec warriors that used the macuahuitl and recruited from all social classes were named after eagles and these animals.
question.answerHtml: jaguars [or ocēlōtl; accept jaguar warriors; accept jaguar knights; prompt on cats]
question.clue: Strange stone statues with cleft heads, such as many found by Matthew Stirling, represent an art motif referred to as a "were- ."

swap.leadin: The first expedition of this type was begun by Tlacaelel after a mutual agreement to begin it at a specific time and place.
swap.text: Name this term for battles undergone in Mesoamerica with the aim of capturing prisoners for human sacrifice. They may have been largely ceremonial.
swap.clue: This planned, ritual conflicts that targeted altepetl ("al-teh-peh-tul") and were conducted partly to use prisoners for human sacrifice.

question.leadin: The ruler of this city, Hunac Ceel, supposedly convinced the ruler at Chichen Itza to steal the bride of Izamal, inciting a war that depopulated Chichen Itza.
question.text: Name this Mesoamerican site in the Yucatan that formed a namesake league of 16 city-states around 1280 AD under the Cocom family, which lasted until the revolt of the Xiu family.

swap.text: The nine books given this name are primary sources on Mayan religious tradition. Among their contents include prophecies and prognostications based on the k'atun cycle and riddles used to confirm public officials for office.

question.text: This civilization sacked the Mayan city of Teotihuacan. They had their capital at Tula, Hidalgo and faced the nomadic Chichimec people.
question.clue: It's not Teotihuacan, but the Mexica ("may-SHE"-kah) passed through the ruins of this culture's capital on their way to settling the Valley of Mexico, which inspired the layout of Tenochtitlan and other Aztec cities.

swap.leadin: The dynasty that ruled Tikal after Siyah K'ak's invasion originated from this city.
swap.text: Name this city ruled by Spearthrower Owl that was the most populous city in Mesoamerica at the time. This city's inhabitants built the Pyramids of the Sun and the Moon.
swap.clue: The decline of this city has been attributed to an increase in power of the "intermediate elites" by archaeologists such as Linda Manzanilla.
